summary.text:
A covering report only — the annual report is Appendix 2 and we do not hold it — so there is no CFR, no internal borrowing figure and no reconciliation. What the covering report does give is two dated, specific things: annual member treasury training in December, hosted by the Governance and Audit Committee, delivered by the advisers, with members expressly invited to ask for topics beforehand; and a live tender to appoint new treasury advisers from September 2026.

The substantive point is paragraph 1.10. They explored rescheduling with their advisers and concluded premiums were too expensive for their portfolio. We hold 75 of their PWLB loans, £313.6m at 4.554%, and on today's curve that is true of part of the book — the six loans at 7.00%–7.13% running to 2055–57 carry about £4.97m of premium between them — and the opposite of true for the rest. 44 loans, £218.8m, sit in discount worth about £25.0m, so the whole book prices roughly £16.8m below par. Their conclusion was about their year and their advisers' analysis; ours is 14 August at notice 314/26. Both can be right.

officer.body:
Hi Chris,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the annual report and Q1 update that went to Governance and Audit on 22 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first, with a caveat. We hold 75 PWLB loans for Flintshire, £313.6m at a weighted 4.554%. That sits inside the £332.2m of long-term borrowing at 4.50% in your paragraph 1.13, with the balance presumably non-PWLB. Our file and your Q1 date aren't the same day, so we'd put that as the shape agreeing rather than a tie to the pound. Worth saying too that we only hold your covering report — Appendix 2 and the portfolio appendices aren't in what we can see — so there's no CFR in anything below and we've asserted nothing about your balance sheet.

Paragraph 1.10 is what we wanted to write about. You explored rescheduling with your advisers and concluded that premiums remained relatively expensive for the loans in the portfolio, so nothing was done. Looking at the same book on the DMO's premature repayment curve this afternoon, notice 314/26, that reads as true of one part of it and the reverse of true for the rest. Thirty of the loans, £90.1m of principal, do carry premium — about £8.19m in total, and roughly £4.97m of that is concentrated in six loans at 7.00% to 7.13% running to 2055, 2056 and 2057. Those are the expensive ones and they will stay expensive. But the other forty-four, £218.8m, price the other way, worth about £25.0m of discount — the largest single one being the £10m at 2.64% out to December 2068, at roughly £4.6m below its balance. Netted, the book prices about £16.8m below par today.

None of that contradicts your paragraph. Your conclusion was about your year and your advisers' analysis of it; ours is one afternoon in August on a curve that has moved since. What it does say is that "is anything worth doing" has a different answer on different days, and it's the sort of question that is easier to keep half an eye on than to commission. We price every council's book daily on the DMO's own formula — 182.5-day denominator, D+1 count, banker's rounding — and yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. Ours is indicative and we say so plainly; the DMO's quote is the only one that binds, and we don't model MRP or the accounting treatment, both of which would matter.

Two other things, both because they're dated. Paragraph 1.05 says the annual member training is scheduled for December, hosted by your committee and delivered by your advisers, and that members are welcome to ask for topics in advance. Our academy is built for exactly that — 115 courses, free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, with free accounts for the whole team. For members ahead of December, Treasury management for councillors and Audit committee scrutiny are the two written for the room your report goes into. For the finance side, PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator and Debt restructuring are the pair that sit behind paragraph 1.10, and Working with treasury advisers may be timely given the tender. To be clear on that last one: we're not an adviser and we're not bidding for anything — the course is about how to get value from whoever you appoint.

And on the market itself, our monthly sector breakdown at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is the other half of the picture for the £25m you fixed in the year. July was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, which tells you how much appetite is around before you need to be in it.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
